Economic Growth, Energy Use, and the Materiality
of Production
An Empirical Appendix to Pierre Campergue’s Corpus on Economic Work
and Money
Mélik Lemariey
2026-05-08
Abstract
This note provides a reproducible empirical appendix to Pierre Campergue’s corpus
on economic Work, Money, Cash, Product, labour, and productive transformation.
Campergue’s work should not be reduced to a simple analogy between thermodynam-
ics and economics. Its central methodological contribution is more precise: it uses
the discipline of thermomechanical formalism to clarify economic variables, distin-
guish accounting flows from productive transformations, and separate the movement
of monetary units from the creation of purchasing power.
The empirical question addressed here is narrower than Campergue’s full theoretical
corpus: do real GDP and energy use remain coupled in publicly available macroeco-
nomic data? Using World Bank World Development Indicators, this note reconstructs
an energy-use proxy from dimensionally coherent series and estimates three ordinary
least squares specifications: a level regression, a log-log regression, and a regression
in annual log changes. The analysis covers the world aggregate and five economies:
China, India, the United States, Germany, and France. Although the requested analy-
sis window was 1965–2023, the effective overlap of the selected World Bank series is
1990–2023.
The world-level results show a strong long-run relationship between real GDP and
reconstructed energy use.
The world log-log elasticity is approximately 1.61 with
R² ≈0.99, while the annual log-change specification remains materially associated
with β ≈0.81 and R² ≈0.66. At the national level, the results are heterogeneous:
China and India exhibit strong long-run coupling, while France and Germany show
much weaker or negative territorial relationships. This pattern is consistent with the
hypothesis that the material basis of growth does not disappear in service economies;
rather, part of it becomes less visible in national statistics through efficiency gains,
structural change, and global value-chain displacement.
The results do not validate Campergue’s complete theoretical system. They provide
a limited, reproducible empirical observation compatible with one of its macroeco-
nomic implications: growth remains materially and energetically conditioned, even
when national accounting makes this materiality difficult to see.
1

Keywords: energy, GDP, economic Work, Money, productivity, Pierre Campergue,
World Bank, materiality of growth, decoupling, productive transformation
1
Introduction
Modern economic debates often treat growth as an abstract monetary or statistical
phenomenon. GDP increases, corporate margins rise, financial valuations expand,
and national accounts appear to describe the economy through flows of currency, ser-
vices, income, and expenditure. Yet production remains physically situated. Goods
must be extracted, transformed, transported, maintained, repaired, cleaned, assem-
bled, and powered. Even in service economies, the apparent immateriality of value
creation often rests on material processes displaced elsewhere in the supply chain.
Pierre Campergue’s corpus addresses this problem at the level of economic language.
His manuscript, Reflections on the Economic Power of Work and the Mechanical
Power of Money, does not simply claim that economics is thermodynamics. Such a
reduction would misrepresent the project. Campergue’s effort is primarily semantic,
analytical, and formal: he seeks to define economic variables precisely, distinguish
supports from values, distinguish labour from economic Work, and distinguish flows
from transformations.
This empirical note does not attempt to prove the full corpus.
Its purpose is nar-
rower. It asks whether publicly available macroeconomic data provide evidence for a
persistent coupling between real GDP and energy use. This question matters because
Campergue’s framework gives central importance to productive transformation and
to the work required to alter productive conditions. If economic growth were fully
decoupled from energy at the world scale, one important macroeconomic intuition
of the corpus would be weakened. If, however, world GDP and energy use remain
strongly associated, the empirical result supports the view that growth remains ma-
terially conditioned, even when this condition is obscured by accounting aggregates
and territorial boundaries.
The note therefore treats the code in this repository as an empirical appendix to the
corpus, not as a proof of the entire theoretical construction.
2
Conceptual background: Campergue’s corpus
Campergue’s manuscript is organized around a set of distinctions that ordinary eco-
nomic language often blurs.
The first distinction is between Cash and Money. Cash is the monetary support: the
unit, sign, inscription, or circulating medium. Money, in Campergue’s terminology,
refers to the economic value or purchasing power carried by that support. This dis-
tinction prevents the creation or movement of monetary units from being confused
with the creation of real purchasing power.
2

The second distinction is between labour and Economic Work. Labour is a task, job,
or activity to be carried out. Economic Work is linked to productive transformation,
productivity, and the conditions under which production becomes faster, cheaper, or
more effective. This distinction is essential: an activity may involve effort without
necessarily creating economic Work in Campergue’s technical sense.
The third distinction is between creation, distribution, and use. Distribution real-
locates what already exists. Creation concerns the emergence or transformation of
economic value. Use concerns consumption, operation, or the practical deployment
of what has been produced. Confusing these operations causes economic reasoning
to treat all monetary movements as equivalent, even when they have very different
effects on productive capacity and purchasing power.
The fourth distinction is between flows and transformations. Conventional accounts
often describe goods, services, and money as flows. Campergue’s point is that flows
are not enough. In the natural sciences, a flow is generally the consequence of an
underlying difference or transformation. By analogy at the level of formal reasoning,
economic flows should be related to transformations in utility, price, productivity,
work, and purchasing power.
This is where the thermomechanical formalism enters. The objective is not to import
physical variables directly into economics. Campergue explicitly requires economic
variables to be defined as economic variables. Thermomechanics is used as a formal
discipline: it forces the analyst to define variables, transformations, constraints, and
conservation-like relations before drawing conclusions.
This note focuses on one limited macroeconomic question derived from that orienta-
tion: whether GDP remains empirically coupled to energy use.
3

The code requests the period 1965–2023. However, after merging the available series
across the selected countries, the effective common observation period is 1990–2023.
3

The run metadata reports 204 observations across six country or area codes: WLD, USA,
FRA, DEU, CHN, and IND.
Energy is reconstructed as:
energy = gdp_ppp_real / gdp_per_energy
This replaces the earlier, weaker construction:
energy = gdp_market_real / gdp_per_energy
The earlier version mixed market-dollar GDP with a PPP-based GDP-per-energy ratio.
The updated reconstruction is dimensionally coherent because both numerator and
denominator are expressed in PPP terms.
This remains a reconstructed energy-use proxy, not an independently downloaded
physical energy series. This limitation is discussed below.
4
Method
For each country or aggregate, the script estimates three ordinary least squares spec-
ifications.
4.1
Level regression
GDP_i,t = α_i + β_i Energy_i,t + ε_i,t
This regression captures the long-run level association between real GDP and recon-
structed energy use. It is visually intuitive but vulnerable to common trends.
4.2
Log-log regression
log(GDP_i,t) = α_i + β_i log(Energy_i,t) + ε_i,t
The coefficient β is interpreted as a long-run elasticity. For example, β = 1.6 means
that, within the observed historical relationship, a 1% increase in reconstructed en-
ergy use is associated with approximately a 1.6% increase in real GDP.
This is not a causal claim.
4.3
Annual log-change regression
Δlog(GDP_i,t) = α_i + β_i Δlog(Energy_i,t) + ε_i,t
This specification is more demanding. It tests whether yearly changes in GDP and
yearly changes in energy use move together, rather than merely showing that two
variables trend upward over several decades.
4

4.4
Rolling elasticity
The script also estimates rolling 15-year log-log elasticities.
These are useful for
observing whether the GDP-energy relation is stable or changes across time.

5.1
World aggregate
The world aggregate shows the strongest and most relevant result for the question
of global decoupling.
In levels, the relationship between real GDP and reconstructed energy use is very
strong, with R² ≈0.987. In log-log form, the elasticity is β ≈1.605 with R² ≈0.991.
This indicates a highly stable long-run association between world real GDP and re-
constructed energy use over 1990–2023.
The annual log-change specification remains significant in economic terms: β ≈0.809
with R² ≈0.661. This is important because it reduces the risk that the result is merely
a visual artefact of two upward-trending series.
The world-level result is therefore consistent with the claim that global economic
growth remains materially and energetically coupled.
5.2
China and India
China and India show strong log-log relationships.
China has β ≈1.659 and R² ≈0.979 in log-log form.
India has β ≈1.459 and R²
≈0.996. These results are consistent with the interpretation that industrialization,
infrastructure build-out, urbanization, and production expansion remain strongly tied
to energy use.
However, China’s annual log-change regression is weaker: β ≈0.277 and R² ≈0.152.
This suggests that China’s long-run trajectory is strongly energy-related, but short-
5

term annual variations involve additional factors: structural change, policy, energy
efficiency, measurement effects, and macroeconomic smoothing.
India’s annual log-change relationship is stronger: β ≈0.831 and R² ≈0.479, sug-
gesting a clearer short-run association between GDP growth and energy growth.
5.3
United States
The United States presents a different pattern. The log-log relationship has β ≈2.527
but only R² ≈0.280, indicating a weak long-run fit in territorial data. However, the
annual log-change regression has β ≈0.567 and R² ≈0.655.
This suggests that annual fluctuations in energy and GDP remain associated, but the
long-run level relation is distorted by changes in economic structure, energy effi-
ciency, service-sector expansion, offshoring, and the changing composition of output.
5.4
France and Germany
France and Germany show the weakest territorial relationships.
France has β ≈0.259 and R² ≈0.012 in log-log form, meaning that the level relation-
ship between national GDP and reconstructed territorial energy use is almost absent
in this specification. Germany has β ≈-1.270 and R² ≈0.611, implying a negative
territorial relationship over the observed period.
These results should not be interpreted as proof that energy no longer matters. A
more plausible interpretation is that national territorial data increasingly fail to cap-
ture the energy basis of consumption and value creation. Mature service economies
may import material and energy-intensive goods while recording high domestic value
added in services, intellectual property, finance, administration, design, distribution,
and corporate margins.
In other words, the national energy-GDP relation can disappear statistically while the
global relation remains strong.
6
Discussion
The results support a distinction between global coupling and territorial decou-
pling.
At the world scale, there is no external economy to which material production can be
displaced. Energy-intensive production may move from one country to another, but
it remains within the global system. Therefore, if GDP and energy remain strongly
coupled globally, the apparent decoupling of some service economies should be inter-
preted cautiously.
At the national scale, a country can appear to decouple GDP from energy for several
reasons:
6

1. It may improve energy efficiency.
2. It may shift from industry to services.
3. It may outsource energy-intensive production.
4. It may import embodied energy in goods.
5. It may record high value added in activities whose material base is located else-
where.
6. It may benefit from global supply chains that conceal production energy outside
national accounts.
This distinction is directly relevant to Campergue’s corpus. If one focuses only on
accounting flows, the economy appears increasingly immaterial. If one focuses on
transformations, the material and energetic base remains visible, but often outside
the national boundary where value is booked.
The empirical results therefore support a careful formulation:
The materiality of growth has not disappeared.
It has become less visible in national accounts.
This does not mean that every unit of GDP requires the same amount of energy as in
the past. Energy efficiency, technological change, and structural transformation are
real. The result is subtler: global growth still appears difficult to describe without ref-
erence to energy use, even when some national economies show apparent territorial
decoupling.
7
Relation to Campergue’s corpus
The empirical analysis should be read as a limited test of a macroeconomic implica-
tion, not as a validation of the full theoretical system.
Campergue’s corpus argues that economic reasoning must distinguish monetary sup-
ports from real value, labour from economic Work, and accounting movement from
productive transformation. The GDP-energy results are compatible with that orien-
tation: they suggest that real economic growth remains connected to material and
energetic transformations.
However, the regressions do not prove:
• the full Work →Money formalism;
• the complete distinction between productive and non-productive agents;
• the proposed transformation equations;
• the validity of all definitions in the corpus;
• causality from energy to GDP;
• the absence of feedback from GDP to energy use.
The results provide empirical support for a narrower statement:
At the world scale, real GDP and energy use remain strongly coupled in the tested data.
This is enough to justify including the code as an empirical appendix to the corpus.
7

8
Limitations
8.1
Reconstructed energy proxy
The energy variable is reconstructed from World Bank GDP per unit of energy use:
energy = gdp_ppp_real / gdp_per_energy
This is dimensionally coherent, but it is not the same as using a fully independent pri-
mary or final energy consumption series. A stronger future version should replicate
the analysis using independent physical energy datasets.
8.2
Endogeneity
GDP and energy are mutually endogenous. Energy enables production, but economic
growth also increases the ability to consume energy. The regressions estimate asso-
ciation, not one-way causality.
8.3
Common trends
Level and log-log regressions can overstate relationships when both variables share
long-run trends. The annual log-change regression partially addresses this issue, but
further econometric testing would be required for stronger causal claims.
8.4
Territorial accounting
National energy use does not capture embodied energy in imports. This is especially
important for service economies and countries with extensive offshored production.
Consumption-based energy accounting would be a valuable extension.
8.5
Data coverage
Although the script requests 1965–2023, the merged dataset covers 1990–2023 for
the selected indicators and countries. Claims should therefore be limited to this ef-
fective period unless additional data sources are introduced.
8.6
Limited country set
The current analysis uses the world aggregate and five countries. A broader panel
would be needed to establish systematic patterns across industrial, post-industrial,
emerging, and resource-exporting economies.
8

9
Reproducibility
The analysis can be reproduced in two steps.
First, download the World Bank sources:
python scripts/download_wb_sources.py --out data/code --raw data/raw
Then run the analysis:
python src/energy_gdp_analysis.py \
--gdp-file data/code/API_NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.csv \
--gdp-ppp-file data/code/API_NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.KD.csv \
--gdp-per-energy-file data/code/API_EG.GDP.PUSE.KO.PP.KD.csv \
--countries WLD,USA,FRA,DEU,CHN,IND \
--start-year 1965 \
--end-year 2023 \
--out output_macro
The script writes:
merged_energy_gdp.csv
regression_summary.csv
rolling_loglog_elasticity.csv

10
Conclusion
This empirical note supports a limited but important claim: in the tested World Bank
data, world real GDP and reconstructed energy use remain strongly coupled over
1990–2023. The world log-log relationship is highly stable, and the annual log-change
relationship remains economically meaningful.
At the same time, the national results are heterogeneous. France and Germany show
weak or negative territorial relationships, while China and India show strong long-
run coupling. This contrast suggests that apparent decoupling at the national level
should not be confused with global dematerialization. It may instead reflect structural
change, energy efficiency, offshoring, and the displacement of material production
into global value chains.
The result is compatible with the central intuition of Campergue’s corpus: economic
value cannot be understood only through monetary flows. A serious analysis must dis-
9

tinguish signs from values, tasks from productive transformations, distribution from
creation, and accounting movement from material production.
A cautious summary is therefore:
The data do not prove Campergue’s complete theoretical corpus.
They do support one empirical implication compatible with it:
at the world scale, growth remains materially and energetically conditioned.
11
